verses.note: Scripture says both that God regretted (here and 1 Samuel 15:11, 35) and that he is not a man that he should change his mind (1 Samuel 15:29, Numbers 23:19), sometimes in the same chapter. Classical theology reads such language as describing God's real opposition to evil in terms human beings can grasp, without implying that God was surprised or that his purpose failed; other theologians give the language more literal weight. All agree the verse forbids picturing God as indifferent.

God binds his future actions to a visible sign and speaks of remembering it. The language is deliberately human, but the point is his faithfulness: God places his own word where he will see it and pledges to act according to it.

The verse shows God's patience. He waits four centuries rather than act before judgment is just, which is the same forbearance the New Testament describes as meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4, 2 Peter 3:9).
God's knowledge is not presented here as abstract all-knowing but as attention: he sees a particular person in a particular place. Psalm 139 develops the same thought in prayer.
The question ties God's power to his promise. God is not described as able to do anything at all in the abstract, but as able to do what he has said, even when nature says otherwise.
Abraham's argument assumes that God's justice is not arbitrary but recognizable: humans made in his image can appeal to it. Deuteronomy 32:4 confesses the same conviction.
God's faithfulness is shown here as the exact match between what he says and what he does. The verse repeats the point twice so that no reader can miss that the birth is the keeping of a word.

Jacob names God's covenant love (chesed) and faithfulness (emet) as the explanation of his whole life. They are the qualities God will proclaim as his name at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), and Jacob confesses them here as things he has received, not earned.

The four verbs describe a God who is attentive, faithful to his word, and personally concerned with human suffering. Remembering, in Scripture, means turning to act on a commitment, not recalling forgotten information.

The God of Exodus is not unmoved by pain. He sees affliction, hears cries, and knows sufferings, and this knowledge leads to action. The verse is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of God's compassion joined to his power.

Christian theology has drawn the doctrine of God's self-existence (often called aseity) partly from this verse: God is not caused, completed, or sustained by anything outside himself. Jesus' words ‘before Abraham was born, I am’ (John 8:58) are widely read as an echo of this self-designation.

God's anger is real, and it is also slow and restrained: he does not reject Moses but provides for his weakness. Later God will describe himself as slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (34:6), and this scene is an early instance of it.

God's jealousy is the zeal of a covenant partner for an exclusive relationship. It is inseparable from his loving devotion: the same God who will not share his people with idols keeps faith with them for a thousand generations. The proportion of the two clauses is itself a statement about his character.

God describes himself, and mercy comes first and at length. Every term but the last is a form of love or grace, and the list became Israel's creed about God's character, quoted by psalmists and prophets across centuries.

Forgiveness and justice stand in the same sentence without canceling each other. The verse leaves the tension unresolved; the rest of Scripture, and for Christians the cross above all (Romans 3:25-26), shows how God can be both the one who forgives and the one who does not declare the guilty innocent.

The same God who has just proclaimed himself compassionate and gracious now calls himself Jealous. The two belong together: God's jealousy is the exclusive devotion of love, which refuses to share the beloved with rivals who would destroy her.
God's jealousy is the other face of his covenant love. A God indifferent to his people's unfaithfulness would not love them in the way the Shema requires them to love him.

The truthfulness of God's word is the foundation of David's hope. The New Testament speaks the same way when Jesus prays that the Father's word is truth (John 17:17) and when Paul says every promise of God finds its Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).
Power and tenderness belong to the same God and are exercised by the same arm. The passage refuses to set God's might against his gentleness: the one who rules is the one who carries the weak.

God's wisdom is underived. He does not learn, consult, or discover; he knows. This is the root of the classical teaching that God's knowledge is not gained from creatures, and it is why his counsel can be trusted when events seem to contradict it.

God is eternal, the Creator of the whole earth, tireless, and unsearchable in understanding. The attributes are not listed for their own sake; each answers the complaint. An everlasting God has not aged out of his promises; a Creator of the ends of the earth is not limited to Judah; a God who does not tire has not given up; and unsearchable understanding means his silence is not ignorance.

God is named great, awesome, and faithful before anything is asked. His covenant loyalty is the fixed point against which Israel's unfaithfulness is measured and the only ground on which the prayer dares to proceed.

Mercy is not presented as an exception God makes to his character but as something that belongs to him, like the righteousness of verse 7. The prayer holds both in God without resolving one into the other.

The Father ‘sees what is done in secret’. God's knowledge reaches what no human observer can, and Jesus turns that truth from a threat into an encouragement: nothing given quietly for him goes unseen.
God's knowledge of our needs precedes our asking. Jesus draws a practical conclusion from God's omniscience: it makes prayer simple, not pointless.

Jesus knows what the scribes are thinking without being told, the knowledge of hearts that Scripture ascribes to God (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Mark presents it without comment, as another sign of who stands in the room.

Jesus' compassion reaches to ordinary physical need and to people with no claim on him, a Gentile crowd far from home. The verse shows God's mercy in the concrete form of worry that people will collapse on the road.

Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone; every other goodness is derived. The saying has been read in two ways: as Jesus deflecting praise in humility, or as a veiled invitation to recognize that the one addressed as good stands on God's side of that line. The church has generally read it in the second way, in light of Mark's portrait of Jesus as the one who forgives sins, which only God can do (2:7).
Luke again shows Jesus knowing hidden thoughts (5:22, 9:47, 11:17), a knowledge the Old Testament ascribes to God, who searches the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10).

Israel confessed the LORD as ‘compassionate and gracious’ (Exodus 34:6). Here the narrator names Jesus ‘the Lord’ in the same breath as he describes his compassion, and the compassion acts unasked. Luke shows God's mercy not as a doctrine about Jesus but as something seen in his face and heard in his first word to a grieving woman.

Jesus' knowledge of Nathanael is the first instance of a pattern in John: he knows what is in people (2:24-25) and knows the Samaritan woman's life (4:17-18). The Gospel presents this as a divine prerogative, since Scripture ascribes such knowledge to God (Psalm 139:1-4).

Scripture says that God alone knows the human heart (1 Kings 8:39, Jeremiah 17:10). John ascribes that knowledge to Jesus without qualification, and he shows it at work in the next chapters, with Nathanael (1:47-48), Nicodemus, and the Samaritan woman (4:18).

God is not bound to a body or a place. The church's teaching that God is spirit, without body, parts, or location, rests heavily on this verse, and it does not make God abstract: the spirit God is the Father who seeks worshipers.

God's kindness, forbearance, and patience are described as riches, an overflowing supply. These are the attributes God proclaimed to Moses (Exodus 34:6), and Paul holds them together with his justice rather than against it.

God's faithfulness does not depend on the faithfulness of his people. His truthfulness is the fixed point by which everything else is measured, so that even human unbelief ends by demonstrating that God keeps his word (2 Timothy 2:13).

The verse is important for the meaning of God's righteousness in Romans: here it is his character as the just judge, not a gift given to believers. Readers weighing 1:17 and 3:21 must reckon with this usage.

Paul raises the question of God's justice himself and refuses to answer it by denying what he has said about election. His answer (verses 15-18) is that mercy, by definition, cannot be owed, so choosing whom to show it to is not injustice.
God's impartiality is basic to Paul's argument. The God who does not judge by status or ancestry (Deuteronomy 10:17, Romans 2:11) is the God who justifies Jew and Gentile alike through faith.

If the causal reading is right, Christ's refusal to exploit his equality with God reveals what God is like: not self-seeking but self-giving. That reading makes the cross not a hiding of God's glory but its display, a theme later developed in Luther's theology of the cross.

The unchangeableness the psalm ascribes to God is ascribed to the Son. What is true of God's eternity is true of him, which is why the letter can later say he is the same yesterday, today, and forever (13:8).
God's knowledge is complete: nothing in creation is hidden from him. The attribute that theology calls omniscience is presented here as personal and moral, the eyes of the one to whom we answer.
It is ‘impossible for God to lie’. The verse grounds Christian hope in God's truthfulness and the unchangeableness of his purpose, the same attributes Numbers 23:19 and Titus 1:2 affirm.
God ‘will not change His mind’. The oath of Psalm 110 is, like the oath to Abraham (6:17), a pledge of God's own constancy, and the whole new covenant rests on it.
